Noise shaping under injection locking and the injection-pulling spectrum

Prerequisites: paper_003 ([P3] generalized Adler, lock characteristic), white_noise_to_phase_noise (the machine that turns white noise into 1/f21/f^21/f2), lorentzian_linewidth (what a free-running oscillator is doing near the carrier) | Next: quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators (mutual injection = two coupled Adler equations), pll_noise_budget (how a second-order loop keeps the books).

paper_003 covered "whether it locks at all" (lock range, stability). This page covers the other two dividends left in that [P3] equation:

What this page answers:

  1. Once locked, where does the oscillator's own phase noise go? How much is it suppressed, and up to what frequency? (Part A)
  2. Why does "still locked" not mean "still clean" — what is this vanishing suppression at the lock edge? (Part A)
  3. When it does not lock (∣Δω∣>ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert \gt \omega_L∣Δω∣>ωL​), what does the spectrum look like? Why a comb of spacing ωb\omega_bωb​, growing on only one side? Where does ωb=Δω2−ωL2\omega_b=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}ωb​=Δω2−ωL2​​ come from? (Part B)

Physical intuition (conclusion first): an injection-locked oscillator is a first-order PLL — the injection supplies a restoring force that pulls the phase back to the lock point, and the strength of that restoring force (units rad/s) is the loop bandwidth. So: self-noise below the frequency the restoring force can track gets flattened (high-pass shaping), reference noise below that same frequency is copied through wholesale (low-pass); the restoring force ωc=ωLcos⁡θss\omega_c=\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}ωc​=ωL​cosθss​ is strongest dead center in the lock range and vanishes at the edges. When it fails to lock, the restoring force loses to the detuning, and the phase slides around in a "dwell-then-slip" sawtooth, spitting out one sideband per revolution — that's the pulling comb spectrum.

Where this page sits: an advanced design page. The phase equation itself ([P3] Eq.(26)/(28)–(30)/(33)–(35)/(38)–(40)) and the beat frequency ([P4] Eq.(31)–(34)) have both been verified against the original PDFs; putting noise into the Adler equation and reading off the shaped PSD is textbook-standard but is not in the derivations of the five source PDFs on this site ([P4] p.2130 explicitly points its noise analysis to its own reference [29, Ch. 7], i.e. Hong's PhD thesis; the classic source is Kurokawa 1973, see the external-literature list at the end); this page derives it from scratch and cross-checks with simulation.

Part A — Noise shaping of a locked oscillator (a first-order PLL)​

Step 1: lock point and the stable branch​

Steady state dθ/dt=0d\theta/dt=0dθ/dt=0 requires sin⁡θss=Δω/ωL\sin\theta_{ss}=\Delta\omega/\omega_Lsinθss​=Δω/ωL​, which exists provided ∣Δω∣≤ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\le\omega_L∣Δω∣≤ωL​ (this is the lock range). There are two solutions:

θss=arcsin⁡ ⁣(ΔωωL)orπ−arcsin⁡ ⁣(ΔωωL).\theta_{ss}=\arcsin\!\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega}{\omega_L}\Big)\quad\text{or}\quad\pi-\arcsin\!\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega}{\omega_L}\Big).θss​=arcsin(ωL​Δω​)orπ−arcsin(ωL​Δω​).

Which one is stable? Following [P3]'s stability criterion (Eq.(38)–(39), p.2115): substitute θ=θ0+θ^\theta=\theta_0+\hat\thetaθ=θ0​+θ^, expand to first order in Taylor series, giving dθ^/dt=Ω′(θ0)θ^d\hat\theta/dt=\Omega'(\theta_0)\hat\thetadθ^/dt=Ω′(θ0​)θ^; stable ⟺ Ω′(θ0)<0\Omega'(\theta_0)\lt0Ω′(θ0​)<0. Here Ω′(θ)=−ωLcos⁡θ\Omega'(\theta)=-\omega_L\cos\thetaΩ′(θ)=−ωL​cosθ, so the stable branch is cos⁡θss>0\cos\theta_{ss}\gt0cosθss​>0, i.e. the principal value θss=arcsin⁡(Δω/ωL)∈(−π/2,π/2)\theta_{ss}=\arcsin(\Delta\omega/\omega_L)\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)θss​=arcsin(Δω/ωL​)∈(−π/2,π/2); the other solution is unstable.

Mechanical analogy: the tilted washboard. The classical Adler equation dθ/dt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetadθ/dt=Δω−ωL​sinθ is exactly the equation of motion of a ball rolling under overdamped dynamics (inertia negligible, velocity proportional to force) in the potential U(θ)=−Δω⋅θ−ωLcos⁡θU(\theta)=-\Delta\omega\cdot\theta-\omega_L\cos\thetaU(θ)=−Δω⋅θ−ωL​cosθ — overdamped particles obey dθ/dt=−dU/dθd\theta/dt=-dU/d\thetadθ/dt=−dU/dθ, and substituting confirms −dU/dθ=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ-dU/d\theta=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta−dU/dθ=Δω−ωL​sinθ ✓. U(θ)U(\theta)U(θ) is a "cosine corrugation" riding on a linear ramp: the ramp's slope is set by Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, the corrugation depth by ωL\omega_LωL​ — hence "tilted washboard." When r≡Δω/ωL<1r\equiv\Delta\omega/\omega_L\lt1r≡Δω/ωL​<1 the ramp is not steep enough to wash out the corrugation, so local dips (wells) remain and the ball falls into one and stops — this is exactly the geometric meaning of θss\theta_{ss}θss​ above. When r>1r\gt1r>1 the ramp overwhelms the corrugation, the wells vanish entirely, and the ball never stops rolling — corresponding to the pulling case in Part B below. The animation below turns this intuition into something you can drive interactively and watch cycle slips happen live:

Reading the animation: the curve is the tilted washboard potential U(θ); the ball's horizontal position is the Adler phase θ, and it always rolls "downhill" (dθ/dt = −dU/dθ = Δω − ω_L sin θ, this page's boxed classical Adler equation). At r = Δω/ω_L < 1 the tilt is gentle enough that U(θ) still has local wells — the ball settles into one and stops: that is lock. At r > 1 the tilt has washed the wells out entirely — the ball rolls forever, one full 2π "slip" per beat period T_b = 2π/ω_b (ω_b = √(Δω²−ω_L²), derived in Part B below). Turning up "noise strength" adds a random-walk kick to dθ/dt each frame; near r ≈ 1 an unlucky kick can shove the ball out of a shallowing well before it would otherwise settle — each such escape is one cycle slip, counted live above.
Model: pedagogical mechanical analogy (overdamped particle in a periodic tilted potential), not a literal circuit. ω_L fixed at 1 (normalized units); Δω = r·ω_L. Numerical integration: explicit Euler sub-stepped 4× per frame for stability; noise is a scaled sum-of-uniforms random-walk term (not exact Gaussian white noise, but statistically close for this illustration).

Step 2: putting noise in and linearizing​

The oscillator's own device noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) runs through the same ISF machine ([P1] Eq.(11); [P3] Eq.(28)'s Γ~⋅i\tilde\Gamma\cdot iΓ~⋅i holds equally for a noise current). For white noise, after ISF-weighted averaging over one period it becomes equivalent to a white frequency-noise (white FM) drive n(t)n(t)n(t) added to the right-hand side of the Adler equation:

dθdt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ+n(t),\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta+n(t),dtdθ​=Δω−ωL​sinθ+n(t),

where n(t)n(t)n(t) [rad/s] has one-sided PSD denoted SnS_nSn​, units rad²/s (= (rad/s)²/Hz). This is exactly the drive that grows the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt of a free-running oscillator: remove the injection (ωL=0\omega_L=0ωL​=0), so ϕ=∫n dt\phi=\int n\,dtϕ=∫ndt, and the transfer-function bookkeeping (one-sided in, one-sided out) gives

Sϕ,free(ω)=Snω2,Sn=Γrms2qmax2 in2‾ΔfS_{\phi,free}(\omega)=\frac{S_n}{\omega^2},\qquad S_n=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}Sϕ,free​(ω)=ω2Sn​​,Sn​=qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​

(the same result as the time-domain derivation in white_noise_to_phase_noise, Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2ω2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2\omega^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​ω2) — the time-domain-/2/2/2-convention branch of it). Canonical numbers (true LC: Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC): Sn=0.5×10−24/10−24=0.5S_n=0.5\times10^{-24}/10^{-24}=0.5Sn​=0.5×10−24/10−24=0.5 rad²/s — this is exactly the value used by lab_26 (with the representative value Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 it would be Sn=0.25S_n=0.25Sn​=0.25 rad²/s). Unit check: (−)2C2⋅A2Hz=A2sC2=1s\dfrac{(-)^2}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{Hz}}=\dfrac{\text{A}^2\text{s}}{\text{C}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\text{s}}C2(−)2​⋅HzA2​=C2A2s​=s1​ (i.e. rad²/s) ✓.

Linearization. When solidly locked, θ\thetaθ only dithers a little around θss\theta_{ss}θss​. Let θ=θss+δθ\theta=\theta_{ss}+\delta\thetaθ=θss​+δθ, sin⁡(θss+δθ)≈sin⁡θss+cos⁡θss⋅δθ\sin(\theta_{ss}+\delta\theta)\approx\sin\theta_{ss}+\cos\theta_{ss}\cdot\delta\thetasin(θss​+δθ)≈sinθss​+cosθss​⋅δθ, and Δω−ωLsin⁡θss=0\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta_{ss}=0Δω−ωL​sinθss​=0 cancels the constant term:

 d(δθ)dt=−ωc δθ+n(t),ωc≡ωLcos⁡θss=ωL2−Δω2 \boxed{\ \frac{d(\delta\theta)}{dt}=-\omega_c\,\delta\theta+n(t),\qquad \omega_c\equiv\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}\ } dtd(δθ)​=−ωc​δθ+n(t),ωc​≡ωL​cosθss​=ωL2​−Δω2​ ​

(the second equality uses cos⁡θss=1−(Δω/ωL)2\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{1-(\Delta\omega/\omega_L)^2}cosθss​=1−(Δω/ωL​)2​, taking the positive root on the stable branch.)

This ωc\omega_cωc​ is not a new object: it is exactly the pull-in frequency ωp:=−Ω′(θ0)\omega_p:=-\Omega'(\theta_0)ωp​:=−Ω′(θ0​) defined at [P3] Eq.(40), p.2115 (substitute Ω′=−ωLcos⁡θ\Omega'=-\omega_L\cos\thetaΩ′=−ωL​cosθ to get it), and it is also ωp=NωL2−Δω2\omega_p=N\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωp​=NωL2​−Δω2​ at [P4] Eq.(32), p.2130, with N=1N=1N=1. [P3] uses it to describe "how fast a perturbation decays" (θ^∝e−t/τp\hat\theta\propto e^{-t/\tau_p}θ^∝e−t/τp​, τp=1/ωp\tau_p=1/\omega_pτp​=1/ωp​); what we're saying now is: the same frequency is the corner of the noise shaping. And this correspondence is general: for any injection waveform, any topology, the noise-shaping corner =−Ω′(θss)=-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})=−Ω′(θss​) — the slope of the lock characteristic at the lock point.

Step 3: the shaped PSD (a first-order Lorentzian)​

Fourier-transforming the linearized equation (δθ→Θ(ω)\delta\theta\to\Theta(\omega)δθ→Θ(ω), n→N(ω)n\to N(\omega)n→N(ω)):

jω Θ=−ωc Θ+N⟹Θ(ω)=N(ω)ωc+jω⟹ Sθ(ω)=Snωc2+ω2 j\omega\,\Theta=-\omega_c\,\Theta+N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Theta(\omega)=\frac{N(\omega)}{\omega_c+j\omega} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\ S_\theta(\omega)=\frac{S_n}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\ }jωΘ=−ωc​Θ+N⟹Θ(ω)=ωc​+jωN(ω)​⟹ Sθ​(ω)=ωc2​+ω2Sn​​ ​

This is the Lorentzian PSD of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Dimension check: rad2/s1/s2=rad2⋅s=rad2/Hz\dfrac{\text{rad}^2/\text{s}}{1/\text{s}^2}=\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{s}=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}1/s2rad2/s​=rad2⋅s=rad2/Hz ✓.

Factor-of-2 discipline: Sθ=Sn/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta=S_n/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​=Sn​/(ωc2​+ω2) is transfer-function bookkeeping "same side in, same side out" — SnS_nSn​ one-sided in gives SθS_\thetaSθ​ one-sided out (this page and its simulations are one-sided throughout); switch to two-sided and both sides just pick up a factor of 1/21/21/2, the formula shape is unchanged. And the suppression ratio Sθ/Sϕ,free=ω2/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta/S_{\phi,free}=\omega^2/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​/Sϕ,free​=ω2/(ωc2​+ω2) cancels SnS_nSn​ entirely — it is independent of any one-sided/two-sided or /2/2/2//4/4/4 convention — the simulation measures the corner from this ratio, which is the cleanest way.

Three limits, three sentences:

  • ω≫ωc\omega\gg\omega_cω≫ωc​: Sθ→Sn/ω2=Sϕ,freeS_\theta\to S_n/\omega^2=S_{\phi,free}Sθ​→Sn​/ω2=Sϕ,free​ — far from the carrier, it is identical to free-running. The restoring force from the injection (bandwidth ωc\omega_cωc​) can't track fast jitter — it has no effect there.
  • ω≪ωc\omega\ll\omega_cω≪ωc​: Sθ␀␀→Sn/ωc2S_\theta\to S_n/\omega_c^2Sθ​→Sn​/ωc2​ = a finite plateau. The free-running 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence as ω→0\omega\to0ω→0 has been "cured" by locking: the phase no longer random-walks — it's pinned to θss\theta_{ss}θss​ with finite dither. (Compare with lorentzian_linewidth: the free-running case turns the divergence into a finite Lorentzian peak via "linewidth," but the variance still grows without bound over time; locking genuinely pins the variance to a constant — two different "cures.")
  • Crossover ω=ωc\omega=\omega_cω=ωc​: the suppression ratio is exactly 1/21/21/2 (−3-3−3 dB) — the operational definition of the corner, and the simulation measures it this way.

Total phase variance (one-sided integral):

σθ2=∫0∞Snωc2+(2πf)2 df=Sn2π⋅π2ωc=Sn4ωc.\sigma_\theta^2=\int_0^\infty \frac{S_n}{\omega_c^2+(2\pi f)^2}\,df =\frac{S_n}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2\omega_c}=\frac{S_n}{4\omega_c}.σθ2​=∫0∞​ωc2​+(2πf)2Sn​​df=2πSn​​⋅2ωc​π​=4ωc​Sn​​.

Numerically (lab_26 case A: Sn=0.5S_n=0.5Sn​=0.5 rad²/s, ωc=2π×5×106\omega_c=2\pi\times5\times10^6ωc​=2π×5×106 rad/s): σθ2=0.5/(4×3.14×107)=3.98×10−9\sigma_\theta^2=0.5/(4\times3.14\times10^7)=3.98\times10^{-9}σθ2​=0.5/(4×3.14×107)=3.98×10−9 rad² → σθ=63.1 μ\sigma_\theta=63.1\ \muσθ​=63.1 μrad; converting to time jitter (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz), σt=σθ/(2πf0)=2.0\sigma_t=\sigma_\theta/(2\pi f_0)=2.0σt​=σθ​/(2πf0​)=2.0 fs. Dimension check: rad²/s ÷ rad/s = rad² ✓; rad ÷ (rad/s) = s ✓. This is the power of locking an oscillator to a clean reference: unbounded accumulated jitter becomes a finite 2 fs dither.

Step 4: what about the reference's noise? (the other half of the first-order PLL)​

If the injection's own phase wanders: iinj=Iinjcos⁡(ωinjt+ψ(t))i_{inj}=I_{inj}\cos(\omega_{inj}t+\psi(t))iinj​=Iinj​cos(ωinj​t+ψ(t)) (ψ\psiψ slowly varying), redo the Step-0 average (product-to-sum, fast term averages out) to get Ω=−ωLsin⁡(θ−ψ)\Omega=-\omega_L\sin(\theta-\psi)Ω=−ωL​sin(θ−ψ), and linearize:

d(δθ)dt=−ωc(δθ−ψ)+n⟹Θ(ω)=ωcωc+jω⏟low-passΨ(ω)+1ωc+jω⏟self FM→shapedN(ω)\frac{d(\delta\theta)}{dt}=-\omega_c(\delta\theta-\psi)+n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Theta(\omega)=\underbrace{\frac{\omega_c}{\omega_c+j\omega}}_{\text{low-pass}}\Psi(\omega)+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\omega_c+j\omega}}_{\text{self FM}\to\text{shaped}}N(\omega)dtd(δθ)​=−ωc​(δθ−ψ)+n⟹Θ(ω)=low-passωc​+jωωc​​​​Ψ(ω)+self FM→shapedωc​+jω1​​​N(ω) Sθ,out=ωc2ωc2+ω2 Sψ+1ωc2+ω2 Sn.S_{\theta,out}=\frac{\omega_c^2}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\,S_\psi+\frac{1}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\,S_n .Sθ,out​=ωc2​+ω2ωc2​​Sψ​+ωc2​+ω21​Sn​.
  • Reference phase noise is low-passed (corner is again ωc\omega_cωc​): below ωc\omega_cωc​ it's copied through fully (faithfully reproducing the reference), above ωc\omega_cωc​ it's rejected.
  • Self-noise is high-passed: relative to free-running N/(jω)N/(j\omega)N/(jω), the ratio is jω/(ωc+jω)j\omega/(\omega_c+j\omega)jω/(ωc​+jω), ∣⋅∣2=ω2/(ωc2+ω2)\lvert\cdot\rvert^2=\omega^2/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)∣⋅∣2=ω2/(ωc2​+ω2).

This is exactly the transfer-function pair of a first-order (type-I) PLL — the same logic as the second-order ∣Hlp∣2/∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2/\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2/∣Hhp​∣2 in this site's lab_13, just with the loop degenerated to first order and bandwidth ωc\omega_cωc​. Block diagram:

Honesty note: ωc\omega_cωc​ as the pull-in frequency is a native result of [P3] Eq.(40). Hanging n(t)n(t)n(t) and ψ(t)\psi(t)ψ(t) on it and reading off the high-pass/low-pass PSD is standard injection-locking noise theory (external literature, not among the five source PDFs: Kurokawa 1973; Razavi 2004 also has an accessible derivation; [P4] p.2130 points its noise analysis to its own reference [29, Ch. 7]).

Degradation at the lock edge (the real design insight)​

ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​'s dependence on Δω\Delta\omegaΔω is an arc: highest at center, dropping vertically at the edges.

  • Δω=0\Delta\omega=0Δω=0: ωc=ωL\omega_c=\omega_Lωc​=ωL​ (corner = the entire half lock range, maximum suppression bandwidth). This also gives [P3] Eq.(35) a second reading: ωL\omega_LωL​ is not just "the range over which it locks" — it is also "the ceiling on the noise-suppression bandwidth" (ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​, equality at dead center).
  • Δω=0.95 ωL\Delta\omega=0.95\,\omega_LΔω=0.95ωL​: cos⁡θss=1−0.952=0.312\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{1-0.95^2}=0.312cosθss​=1−0.952​=0.312, ωc\omega_cωc​ is down to 31%, the low-frequency plateau is raised by 1/cos⁡2θss=10.3×1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}=10.3\times1/cos2θss​=10.3× (+10.1+10.1+10.1 dB) — still locked, but already dirty.
  • Δω→±ωL\Delta\omega\to\pm\omega_LΔω→±ωL​: cos⁡θss→0\cos\theta_{ss}\to0cosθss​→0, ωc→0\omega_c\to0ωc​→0, suppression vanishes entirely; and the linearization itself breaks down (the potential well of the restoring force shallows out, noise starts kicking out cycle slips, transitioning toward Part B's pulling spectrum).

In one sentence: the edge of the lock range is not a wall, it's a ramp — you start paying the phase-noise price well before you actually lose lock. When PVT drifts ω0\omega_0ω0​, Δω\Delta\omegaΔω quietly walks toward the edge, and the phase-noise plateau rises as 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​ — this often bites earlier than "losing lock" itself. What you want to watch in design is the margin in Δω/ωL\Delta\omega/\omega_LΔω/ωL​, e.g. ∣Δω∣≤0.5 ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\le0.5\,\omega_L∣Δω∣≤0.5ωL​ keeps ωc≥0.87 ωL\omega_c\ge0.87\,\omega_Lωc​≥0.87ωL​ (plateau penalty only +1.2+1.2+1.2 dB).

Part B — When it doesn't lock: the injection-pulling spectrum​

Step 1: no steady state, only "dwell-then-slip"​

When ∣Δω∣>ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\gt\omega_L∣Δω∣>ωL​ (discuss Δω>ωL>0\Delta\omega\gt\omega_L\gt0Δω>ωL​>0),

dθdt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ ≥ Δω−ωL > 0\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta\ \ge\ \Delta\omega-\omega_L\ \gt\ 0dtdθ​=Δω−ωL​sinθ ≥ Δω−ωL​ > 0

is positive everywhere: θ\thetaθ rises monotonically, never stopping — locking fails, but the rise is highly non-uniform:

  • Slowest near θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (sin⁡θ=1\sin\theta=1sinθ=1): dθ/dt=Δω−ωLd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_Ldθ/dt=Δω−ωL​. The oscillator "almost locks" and dwells at the phase closest to lock (quasi-lock) — the description at [P3] Sec. V-G, p.2115–2116: spends a considerable amount of time "trying" to lock.
  • Fastest near θ=−π/2\theta=-\pi/2θ=−π/2: dθ/dt=Δω+ωLd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega+\omega_Ldθ/dt=Δω+ωL​ — rapid slip, sweeping through a full revolution in one burst.

So θ(t)\theta(t)θ(t) is a sawtooth staircase of "plateau + steep ramp" (see the simulation plot (a) below), net-sliding 2π2\pi2π per "beat."

Step 2: the beat frequency ωb\omega_bωb​ — derived step by step​

The period of one beat is the time for θ\thetaθ to traverse 2π2\pi2π. Separate variables:

Tb=∫0Tbdt=∫−ππdθΔω−ωLsin⁡θ.T_b=\int_0^{T_b}dt=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta}.Tb​=∫0Tb​​dt=∫−ππ​Δω−ωL​sinθdθ​.

Use the Weierstrass half-angle substitution u=tan⁡(θ/2)u=\tan(\theta/2)u=tan(θ/2) (θ:−π→π\theta:-\pi\to\piθ:−π→π corresponds to u:−∞→∞u:-\infty\to\inftyu:−∞→∞), sin⁡θ=2u1+u2\sin\theta=\dfrac{2u}{1+u^2}sinθ=1+u22u​, dθ=2 du1+u2d\theta=\dfrac{2\,du}{1+u^2}dθ=1+u22du​:

Tb=∫−∞∞1Δω−ωL2u1+u2⋅2 du1+u2=∫−∞∞2 duΔω(1+u2)−2ωLu=∫−∞∞2 duΔω u2−2ωLu+Δω(complete the square in the denominator)=∫−∞∞2 duΔω(u−ωLΔω)2+Δω2−ωL2Δω=2Δω2−ωL2[arctan⁡(Δω u−ωLΔω2−ωL2)]−∞∞=2Δω2−ωL2⋅π.\begin{aligned} T_b&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\Delta\omega-\omega_L\frac{2u}{1+u^2}}\cdot\frac{2\,du}{1+u^2} =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2\,du}{\Delta\omega(1+u^2)-2\omega_L u}\\[4pt] &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2\,du}{\Delta\omega\,u^2-2\omega_L u+\Delta\omega} \qquad\text{(complete the square in the denominator)}\\[4pt] &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2\,du}{\Delta\omega\Big(u-\frac{\omega_L}{\Delta\omega}\Big)^2+\frac{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}{\Delta\omega}} =\frac{2}{\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}}\Big[\arctan\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega\,u-\omega_L}{\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}}\Big)\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}\\[4pt] &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}}\cdot\pi . \end{aligned}Tb​​=∫−∞∞​Δω−ωL​1+u22u​1​⋅1+u22du​=∫−∞∞​Δω(1+u2)−2ωL​u2du​=∫−∞∞​Δωu2−2ωL​u+Δω2du​(complete the square in the denominator)=∫−∞∞​Δω(u−ΔωωL​​)2+ΔωΔω2−ωL2​​2du​=Δω2−ωL2​​2​[arctan(Δω2−ωL2​​Δωu−ωL​​)]−∞∞​=Δω2−ωL2​​2​⋅π.​

(The second-to-last step uses ∫dua(u−u0)2+c=1acarctan⁡(a/c (u−u0))\int\frac{du}{a(u-u_0)^2+c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ac}}\arctan\big(\sqrt{a/c}\,(u-u_0)\big)∫a(u−u0​)2+cdu​=ac​1​arctan(a/c​(u−u0​)), with a=Δω>0a=\Delta\omega\gt0a=Δω>0, c=(Δω2−ωL2)/Δω>0c=(\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2)/\Delta\omega\gt0c=(Δω2−ωL2​)/Δω>0, and arctan⁡\arctanarctan spans π\piπ over the full range.)

 ωb≡2πTb=Δω2−ωL2 ([P4] Eq.(34), p.2130, taking N=1)\boxed{\ \omega_b\equiv\frac{2\pi}{T_b}=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}\ } \qquad\text{([P4] Eq.(34), p.2130, taking }N=1\text{)} ωb​≡Tb​2π​=Δω2−ωL2​​ ​([P4] Eq.(34), p.2130, taking N=1)

The same substitution also gives the closed-form solution in the unlocked regime (equivalent to the ideal-LC special case of [P4] Eq.(33), p.2130):

tan⁡θ(t)2=ωLΔω+ωbΔωtan⁡ωb(t−t0)2.\tan\frac{\theta(t)}{2}=\frac{\omega_L}{\Delta\omega}+\frac{\omega_b}{\Delta\omega}\tan\frac{\omega_b (t-t_0)}{2}.tan2θ(t)​=ΔωωL​​+Δωωb​​tan2ωb​(t−t0​)​.

Units: rad/s ✓ (Δω,ωL\Delta\omega,\omega_LΔω,ωL​ share units, take the square root of the squared difference). Two limits:

  • Δω≫ωL\Delta\omega\gg\omega_LΔω≫ωL​: ωb→Δω\omega_b\to\Delta\omegaωb​→␀Δω — the sideband spacing approaches the detuning itself, the injection degenerates into a single small spur, the oscillator is essentially free-running ✓ (self-consistency check).
  • Δω→ωL+\Delta\omega\to\omega_L^+Δω→ωL+​: ωb→0\omega_b\to0ωb​→0 — critical slowing down: the dwell segment stretches without bound, the beat frequency vanishes, all comb teeth collapse toward the injection frequency — this is the instant of "locking." Note it and Part A's ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​ are two sides of the same square root: inside lock it's called the pull-in frequency, outside lock it's called the beat frequency ([P4] Eq.(32) vs Eq.(34) — a Pythagorean pair).

Numerically (lab_27 uses a 3-4-5 right triangle, verifiable by mental arithmetic): Δf=100\Delta f=100Δf=100 kHz, fL=60f_L=60fL​=60 kHz → fb=1002−602=80f_b=\sqrt{100^2-60^2}=80fb​=1002−602​=80 kHz.

Step 3: spectral structure — comb spacing ωb\omega_bωb​, one edge pinned to the injection​

θ\thetaθ nets 2π2\pi2π every TbT_bTb​, so θ(t)=ωbt+p(t)\theta(t)=\omega_b t+p(t)θ(t)=ωb​t+p(t), with ppp periodic of period TbT_bTb​. The output voltage

V(t)=cos⁡(ωinjt+θ(t))V(t)=\cos\big(\omega_{inj}t+\theta(t)\big)V(t)=cos(ωinj​t+θ(t))

has an analytic signal containing ejθ=ejωbtejp(t)e^{j\theta}=e^{j\omega_b t}e^{jp(t)}ejθ=ejωb​tejp(t), and the Fourier series of ejp(t)e^{jp(t)}ejp(t) has only components at kωbk\omega_bkωb​ — so the spectrum is a comb of spacing ωb\omega_bωb​, with lines at

ω=ωinj+k ωb,k∈Z,\omega=\omega_{inj}+k\,\omega_b,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z},ω=ωinj​+kωb​,k∈Z,

where the k=0k=0k=0 line falls exactly at the injection frequency ([P4] Sec. V-B, p.2130: the tone at one edge of the spectrum always occurs right at the injection frequency). The oscillator's average frequency is ωinj+ωb\omega_{inj}+\omega_bωinj​+ωb​ (near the k=1k=1k=1 main line), which lies between ωinj\omega_{inj}ωinj​ and ω0\omega_0ω0​: it has been "pulled" away from free-running by Δω−ωb\Delta\omega-\omega_bΔω−ωb​ (lab_27 numbers: 100−80=20100-80=20100−80=20 kHz) — this is exactly where the name "pulling" comes from. Detail worth noting ([P3] footnote 18, p.2116): unless ωinj\omega_{inj}ωinj​ happens to be an integer multiple of ωb\omega_bωb​, V(t)V(t)V(t) itself is not a periodic signal — pulling fundamentally destroys the oscillator's periodicity.

The interactive widget below integrates the Adler ODE right in your browser (RK2), takes an FFT of V(t)=cos⁡(ωinjt+θ(t))V(t)=\cos(\omega_{inj}t+\theta(t))V(t)=cos(ωinj​t+θ(t)), and lets you slide r=Δω/ωLr=\Delta\omega/\omega_Lr=Δω/ωL​ from locked into pulling with your own hands, watching the spectrum morph from "a single tone" into "a one-sided comb"; the measured ωb\omega_bωb​ is compared live against the closed form Δω2−ωL2\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}Δω2−ωL2​​ derived above:

Slide r = Δω/ω_L below 1 and the spectrum collapses to a single clean line at ω_inj — the oscillator is locked onto the injection, θ(t) has settled to a constant, so V(t) = cos(ω_inj t + θ_ss) is a pure tone. Model: RK2 (midpoint) integration of dθ/dt = Δω − ω_L·sin(θ) for 4096 steps (dt = 0.02, ω_L = 1 normalized), Hann-windowed FFT of V(t) = cos(ω_inj t + θ(t)) over the last {1024 or 2048}-point window (radix-2 Cooley–Tukey, written inline, no external deps), peak positions refined with parabolic interpolation. Offline verification (Node/Python, same algorithm): at r = 1.5 the measured comb spacing matches √(Δω²−ω_L²) to within ≈0.1% using the 2048-point FFT — see the write-up in Part B and lab_27 for the reference numbers.

Step 4: why is it "one-sided"?​

Physical argument. The instantaneous frequency is

ωosc(t)=ωinj+dθdt∈[ ωinj+Δω−ωL, ωinj+Δω+ωL ],\omega_{osc}(t)=\omega_{inj}+\frac{d\theta}{dt}\in[\,\omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega-\omega_L,\ \omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega+\omega_L\,],ωosc​(t)=ωinj​+dtdθ​∈[ωinj​+Δω−ωL​, ωinj​+Δω+ωL​],

and the entire range sits on the same side of the injection (Δω>ωL\Delta\omega\gt\omega_LΔω>ωL​ guarantees a positive lower bound). And the time-weighting is extremely skewed: θ\thetaθ dwells longest in the dwell segment (ωosc≈ωinj+Δω−ωL\omega_{osc}\approx\omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega-\omega_Lωosc​≈ωinj​+Δω−ωL​, closest to the injection), while the slip segment flashes by — so spectral energy piles up on "the side of the injection frequency toward ω0\omega_0ω0​," hugging the injection and decaying outward; the other side of the injection is nearly empty. This contrasts sharply with symmetric FM (sinusoidal phase modulation → symmetric Bessel sidebands): the phase-modulating waveform of pulling is a sawtooth, not a sinusoid.

Rigorous argument (advanced, one paragraph). Let z=ejθz=e^{j\theta}z=ejθ; the Adler equation becomes the Riccati equation z˙=jΔω z−ωL2(z2−1)\dot z=j\Delta\omega\,z-\tfrac{\omega_L}{2}(z^2-1)z˙=jΔωz−2ωL​​(z2−1). The Riccati solution is a Möbius (fractional-linear) transform of coefficients, letting us write the periodic solution as z=c+d w1+b wz=\dfrac{c+d\,w}{1+b\,w}z=1+bwc+dw​ (w=ejωbtw=e^{j\omega_b t}w=ejωb​t, ∣b∣<1\lvert b\rvert\lt1∣b∣<1); expanding the geometric series 11+bw=∑k(−b)kwk\dfrac{1}{1+bw}=\sum_k(-b)^k w^k1+bw1​=∑k​(−b)kwk leaves only powers k≥0k\ge0k≥0 — so in this idealized Adler model the comb is strictly one-sided, and the amplitudes decay geometrically, with ratio

r=ωLΔω+ωbr=\frac{\omega_L}{\Delta\omega+\omega_b}r=Δω+ωb​ωL​​

(power drops by r2r^2r2 per line). This closed-form spectrum is a standard result (external literature, not among the five source PDFs: Armand 1969, see the end of this page); the rest of this page verifies it numerically with simulation. lab_27's 3-4-5 parameters: r=60/(100+80)=1/3r=60/(100+80)=1/3r=60/(100+80)=1/3, i.e. 20log⁡103=9.5420\log_{10}3=9.5420log10​3=9.54 dB per line.

lab_27: integrating the unlocked Adler ODE → FFT​

Model: RK4 integration of dθ/dt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetadθ/dt=Δω−ωL​sinθ (deterministic; noise turned off to isolate the pulling comb itself), building V(t)=cos⁡(ωinjt+θ(t))V(t)=\cos(\omega_{inj}t+\theta(t))V(t)=cos(ωinj​t+θ(t)), then a Hann-windowed FFT.

Core code (full script: simulations/lab_27_pulling_spectrum.py):

def rhs(th):                                   # unlocked Adler ([P3] Eq.(30) sinusoidal reduction)
    return DW - OMEGA_L*np.sin(th)             # [rad/s]
# ... RK4 integration to get theta[k] ...
V    = np.cos(OMEGA_INJ*t + theta)             # the pulled output voltage
spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(V*np.hanning(V.size)))**2

How to read this figure: (a) θ/2π\theta/2\piθ/2π climbs one step per beat, the flat segments are the quasi-lock dwell; (b) the instantaneous frequency spends most of its time pinned near 1.04 MHz (finj+Δf−fLf_{inj}+\Delta f-f_Lfinj​+Δf−fL​, the "dwell frequency" closest to injection), with brief excursions to 1.16 MHz; (c) spectrum: the red dashed line = injection at 1.000 MHz (the comb's edge), the gray dashed line = free-running at 1.100 MHz (no line there anymore — it's been pulled away), green ▽ = theoretical positions finj+k fbf_{inj}+k\,f_bfinj​+kfb​; the injection's left side is completely clean — the one-sided comb is the clearest fingerprint of pulling.

Injection waveform design: the ceiling on the lock range ([P3] Sec. VI, Cauchy–Schwarz)​

One of Part A's conclusions is that ωL\omega_LωL​ is not just "the range within which you can lock" — it is also the ceiling on the noise-suppression bandwidth (ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​). So "for the same injection power, how far can ωL\omega_LωL​ be pushed" is a real-money design question. [P3] Sec. VI (pp. 2119–2120) gives an answer clean enough to memorize; this section re-derives it step by step, following the paper, and verifies it numerically on three ISFs.

Physical intuition (conclusion first): the ISF is the dashboard showing "how persuadable the oscillator is right now." A fixed current budget should be spent entirely at the phases where ∣Γ~∣\lvert\tilde\Gamma\rvert∣Γ~∣ is large (where the node voltage transitions are steepest and the phase is easiest to push), and not a cent at the phases where Γ~≈0\tilde\Gamma\approx0Γ~≈0. A sinusoidal injection cannot do this — it is forced to spread its money uniformly across the whole period. The optimum is to "shape the injection waveform like the ISF itself" ([P3] Fig. 18, p.2118's concept cartoon).

Step 0: define "how big" the injection is — why rms?​

To compare waveforms of different shapes, you first need a common measuring stick for "equally big." A multi-harmonic waveform has no unique "amplitude," so [P3] uses the rms injection current ([P3] Eq.(43), p.2119, verbatim):

Irms≡⟨iinj2⟩:=1Tinj∫Tinjiinj(t)2 dt .I_{rms}\equiv\sqrt{\langle i_{inj}^2\rangle}:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}i_{inj}(t)^2\,dt}\ .Irms​≡⟨iinj2​⟩​:=Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​iinj​(t)2dt​ .

Units: A2=A\sqrt{\text{A}^2}=\text{A}A2​=A ✓. Why is rms the right proxy for "power"? [P3] p.2119 + Fig. 17: a practical injection circuit is usually a differential pair commutating a static tail current IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​; the instantaneous ∣iinj∣\lvert i_{inj}\rvert∣iinj​∣ is capped by the tail current, so Irms≤IbiasI_{rms}\le I_{bias}Irms​≤Ibias​, and the injection circuit's average power consumption is at least IrmsVDDI_{rms}V_{DD}Irms​VDD​ — fixing IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ ≈ fixing the floor of the injection circuit's power, and it is well-defined for any waveform.

The three-step derivation: inner product → Cauchy–Schwarz → equality condition​

Step 1: the lock range is the extremum of an inner product. The starting point is again the verified lock characteristic ([P3] Eq.(33), p.2114):

Ω(θ)=1Tinj∫TinjΓ~(ωinjt+θ) iinj(t) dt.\Omega(\theta)=\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)\,dt .Ω(θ)=Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~(ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt.

At fixed θ\thetaθ this is precisely the time-averaged inner product of two periodic signals, ⟨u,v⟩=1T∫Tuv dt\langle u,v\rangle=\frac{1}{T}\int_T uv\,dt⟨u,v⟩=T1​∫T​uvdt, with uθ(t)=Γ~(ωinjt+θ)u_\theta(t)=\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)uθ​(t)=Γ~(ωinj​t+θ) [rad/C] and v(t)=iinj(t)v(t)=i_{inj}(t)v(t)=iinj​(t) [A]. The lock condition (the generalization of Part A's Step 1; the steady state of [P3] Eq.(38)) is that Δω\Delta\omegaΔω falls within the range of Ω\OmegaΩ: the upper/lower lock edges are max⁡θΩ\max_\theta\Omegamaxθ​Ω and min⁡θΩ\min_\theta\Omegaminθ​Ω. So "make the lock range big" = "make the extrema of this inner product big" — the circuit problem has become a functional inequality.

Step 2: the Cauchy–Schwarz bound. For every θ\thetaθ and every waveform (the integral form of Cauchy–Schwarz: ∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥ ∥v∥\lvert\langle u,v\rangle\rvert\le\lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥∥v∥):

∣Ω(θ)∣  ≤  1Tinj ⁣∫Tinj ⁣Γ~2(ωinjt+θ) dt⏟= Γ~rms (independent of θ)⋅1Tinj ⁣∫Tinj ⁣iinj2(t) dt⏟= Irms (Eq.(43))\lvert\Omega(\theta)\rvert\;\le\;\underbrace{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{T_{inj}}\!\int_{T_{inj}}\!\tilde\Gamma^2(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,dt}}_{=\ \tilde\Gamma_{rms}\ \text{(independent of }\theta\text{)}}\cdot\underbrace{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{T_{inj}}\!\int_{T_{inj}}\!i_{inj}^2(t)\,dt}}_{=\ I_{rms}\ \text{(Eq.(43))}}∣Ω(θ)∣≤=␀ Γ~rms​ (independent of θ)Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~2(ωinj​t+θ)dt​​​⋅= Irms​ (Eq.(43))Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​iinj2​(t)dt​​​

The first factor is independent of θ\thetaθ: one injection period sweeps the entire 2π2\pi2π of Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ exactly once, and a mean square does not care at which phase the sweep starts. Units: rad/C×A=rad/s\text{rad/C}\times\text{A}=\text{rad/s}rad/C×A=rad/s ✓. Therefore, no matter what shape you give the waveform, the lock range can never exceed ([P3] Eq.(45), p.2120, verbatim)

ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms .\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}\ .ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​ .

Step 3: the equality condition — the waveform = the shape of the ISF. Cauchy–Schwarz holds with equality ⟺ the two "vectors" are parallel: iinj(t)=λ Γ~(ωinjt+const)i_{inj}(t)=\lambda\,\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\text{const})iinj​(t)=λΓ~(ωinj​t+const). Normalizing the size of λ\lambdaλ to the given IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ via Eq.(43) gives the optimal injection waveform ([P3] Eq.(44), p.2119, verbatim; x=ωinjtx=\omega_{inj}tx=ωinj​t is the linear injection phase):

iinj,0∗(x)=±IrmsΓ~rms Γ~(x) .i_{inj,0}^{*}(x)=\pm\frac{I_{rms}}{\tilde\Gamma_{rms}}\,\tilde\Gamma(x)\ .iinj,0∗​(x)=±Γ~rms​Irms​​Γ~(x) .

Three key points:

  • With the + sign, Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) becomes the ISF's autocorrelation × Irms/Γ~rms\times\,I_{rms}/\tilde\Gamma_{rms}×Irms​/Γ~rms​, reaching +IrmsΓ~rms+I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}+Irms​Γ~rms​ at the aligned point — optimizing the upper lock edge; the − sign likewise optimizes the lower edge ([P3] p.2120 states it explicitly: the positive solution for the upper edge, the negative for the lower). One waveform cannot push both edges to the ceiling simultaneously — see the numbers in Check 2 below.
  • No manual alignment needed: θ\thetaθ is the oscillator's own degree of freedom; the locking mechanism adjusts it onto the stable branch satisfying Δω=Ω(θ)\Delta\omega=\Omega(\theta)Δω=Ω(θ). Waveform design only needs the shape right — the phase is found by the physics itself.
  • Factor bookkeeping: Eq.(45) contains no 2 and no 4 — both sides are rms quantities. The 12\tfrac1221​ in the classical sinusoidal result ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣ ([P3] Eq.(35)) is the projection integral ⟨cos⁡2⟩=12\langle\cos^2\rangle=\tfrac12⟨cos2⟩=21​, with IinjI_{inj}Iinj​ a peak value; rewritten in rms (Irms=Iinj/2I_{rms}=I_{inj}/\sqrt2Irms​=Iinj​/2​) it reads ωL,sine=Irms∣Γ~1∣/2\omega_{L,sine}=I_{rms}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert/\sqrt2ωL,sine​=Irms​∣Γ~1​∣/2​. All of these 2\sqrt22​'s and 222's are peak↔rms conversions and projection constants — nothing to do with the SSB /2/2/2, /4/4/4 bookkeeping conventions.

Check 1: pure-sine ISF — a sinusoidal injection is "already" optimal (the ratio must be 1)​

The ideal LC's Γ~(x)=−sin⁡(x)/qmax\tilde\Gamma(x)=-\sin(x)/q_{max}Γ~(x)=−sin(x)/qmax​ is itself a single-tone sinusoid, so the waveform "shaped like the ISF" is a sine — the theorem predicts a sinusoidal injection already sits at the ceiling. Compute both sides (the true-LC Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ branch, not the representative value 0.5):

ωL,sine=Irms∣Γ~1∣2=Irms2 qmax,ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms=Irms2 qmax⇒ratio=1.\omega_{L,sine}=\frac{I_{rms}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert}{\sqrt2}=\frac{I_{rms}}{\sqrt2\,q_{max}},\qquad \omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}=\frac{I_{rms}}{\sqrt2\,q_{max}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\text{ratio}=1 .ωL,sine​=2​Irms​∣Γ~1​∣​=2​qmax​Irms​​,ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​=2​qmax​Irms​​⇒ratio=1.

Numbers (reusing Part A's canonical case: qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, peak 62.83 μ62.83\ \mu62.83 μA i.e. Irms=44.43 μI_{rms}=44.43\ \muIrms​=44.43 μA): ωL∗=4.443×10−5×0.7071/10−12=3.14×107\omega_L^*=4.443\times10^{-5}\times0.7071/10^{-12}=3.14\times10^7ωL∗​=4.443×10−5×0.7071/10−12=3.14×107 rad/s → fL∗=5.000f_L^*=5.000fL∗​=5.000 MHz, identical to Part A's sinusoidal lock range. Dimension check: A × rad/C = (C/s)(rad/C) = rad/s ✓. (The simulation prints f_L sine = 5.0000 MHz, f_L matched = 5.0000 MHz, gain = 1.0000.)

Teaching point: this is no coincidence — it is forced by "the ISF has only one harmonic." The only thing a sinusoidal injection can buy is Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​, and a pure-sine ISF keeps all of its rms in Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​. For waveform design to "make money," the ISF must hide energy where a sine cannot reach: DC (c0c_0c0​) or higher harmonics. The next two checks demonstrate one of each.

Check 2: asymmetric toy ISF — matched injection profits at DC (and only on one edge)​

The site toy Γ(θ)=cos⁡θ+0.3\Gamma(\theta)=\cos\theta+0.3Γ(θ)=cosθ+0.3 (α=0.3\alpha=0.3α=0.3, DC value c0/2=0.3c_0/2=0.3c0​/2=0.3): Γrms=α2+12=0.7681\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\alpha^2+\tfrac12}=0.7681Γrms​=α2+21​​=0.7681, c1=1c_1=1c1​=1. Closed-form gain:

G=ωL∗ωL,sine=IrmsΓrms/qmaxIrms c1/(2 qmax)=2 Γrmsc1=1+2α2=1.0863.G=\frac{\omega_L^*}{\omega_{L,sine}}=\frac{I_{rms}\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}}{I_{rms}\,c_1/(\sqrt2\,q_{max})}=\frac{\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{rms}}{c_1}=\sqrt{1+2\alpha^2}=1.0863 .G=ωL,sine​ωL∗​​=Irms​c1​/(2​qmax​)Irms​Γrms​/qmax​​=c1​2​Γrms​​=1+2α2​=1.0863.

(Simulation: gain = 1.0863, fLf_LfL​ from 5.0000 → 5.4314 MHz.) The matched waveform is just the shape of cos⁡+α\cos+\alphacos+α — the extra DC share of the current couples to the ISF's c0c_0c0​, something a zero-mean sine can never buy. But note the one-sidedness (the ±\pm± choice): in units of Irms/qmaxI_{rms}/q_{max}Irms​/qmax​, the simulation prints matched(+) upper/lower edges =+0.7681=+0.7681=+0.7681/−0.5338-0.5338−0.5338, versus the sine's ±0.7071\pm0.7071±0.7071 — the upper edge gains 8.6% while the lower edge loses 24%; for the lower edge, switch to the −-− sign. The DC injection shifts the whole lock characteristic upward — exactly the mechanism by which "the upper and lower lock edges can have the same sign," as the caption of [P3] Fig. 10 notes.

Check 3: ring-style narrow-pulse ISF — gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​, ≈ ×2 at 17 stages​

A ring's ISF energy concentrates at the transitions. As a toy, use the [P2] App.B triangular-pulse construction (A=1A=1A=1, symmetric rise/fall): two opposite-sign triangular pulses, height h=1/f′h=1/f'h=1/f′, half-width w=1/f′w=1/f'w=1/f′ rad, with f′=ηN/πf'=\eta N/\pif′=ηN/π (from [P2] Eq.(54), p.803 with A=1A=1A=1). Sanity check: this construction's Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ lands exactly back on [P2] Eq.(55) (A=1A=1A=1): the simulation prints 0.05634 = the closed form 2π2/3η3/N1.5=\sqrt{2\pi^2/3\eta^3}/N^{1.5}=2π2/3η3​/N1.5= 0.05634 ✓.

The narrow-pulse closed-form gain (three lines): a single pulse of area hwhwhw gives c1≈2hw/πc_1\approx 2hw/\pic1​≈2hw/π (the two opposite-sign pulses sit π\piπ apart, so their projections onto sin⁡\sinsin add with the same sign); Γrms2=12π⋅2⋅23h2w=2h2w3π\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\cdot2\cdot\tfrac23h^2w=\tfrac{2h^2w}{3\pi}Γrms2​=2π1​⋅2⋅32​h2w=3π2h2w​; substituting h=w=1/f′h=w=1/f'h=w=1/f′, f′=ηN/πf'=\eta N/\pif′=ηN/π:

G=2 Γrmsc1≈2⋅2h2w3π4h2w2π2=π3w=ηN3 .G=\frac{\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{rms}}{c_1}\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot\frac{2h^2w}{3\pi}}{\frac{4h^2w^2}{\pi^2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3w}}=\sqrt{\frac{\eta N}{3}}\ .G=c1​2​Γrms​​≈π24h2w2​2⋅3π2h2w​​​=3wπ​​=3ηN​​ .

N=17N=17N=17, η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75: G=4.25=2.0616G=\sqrt{4.25}=2.0616G=4.25​=2.0616 (full numerical simulation 2.0720; the 0.5% difference is the sinc2\mathrm{sinc}^2sinc2 correction for the pulses' finite width). With units attached: for the same Irms=44.43 μI_{rms}=44.43\ \muIrms​=44.43 μA and qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, sine 192.3 kHz → matched 398.4 kHz.

This ×2 is not the toy congratulating itself: [P3] Fig. 19 (p.2119) runs transistor-level simulations of a 17-stage single-ended ring — injecting pulses shaped close to the ISF (Fig. 19(b), not a strict ISF replica), and p.2120 states verbatim: "the lock range is almost doubled compared to a sinusoidal injection of the same power." The toy's ηN/3≈2.06\sqrt{\eta N/3}\approx2.06ηN/3​≈2.06 agrees with the real circuit's "almost doubled" at the level of the factor 2, not the decimals (the real ISF's details differ). The gain is ∝N\propto\sqrt N∝N​: more stages → transitions occupy a smaller fraction of the phase → the sine wastes more — long rings are where waveform design pays off the most.

An honest toy footnote: the site's cruder gamma_triangular toy is π\piπ-periodic (the rising and falling triangles repeat perfectly symmetrically), so it has even harmonics only — the simulation prints its c1=0.000000c_1=0.000000c1​=0.000000, c2=0.3625c_2=0.3625c2​=0.3625: a fundamental-frequency sine cannot lock it at all (effectively only superharmonic injection would work). This is a toy artifact (a real ring's rising and falling edges are never so symmetric that only even harmonics survive), but it demonstrates the same lesson in the most extreme way: a sine can only buy c1c_1c1​; if the ISF puts no energy in c1c_1c1​, the money is wasted.

lab_33: numerical verification + figure​

Model: on a 4096-point phase grid, write the periodic average of [P3] Eq.(33) as a circular correlation; for each of the three ISFs compute the lock characteristic under a sinusoidal and a matched injection (same IrmsI_{rms}Irms​); the extrema are the lock edges.

Core code (full script: simulations/lab_39_optimal_injection.py):

def lock_characteristic(gt, i_wave):                  # [P3] Eq.(33): circular correlation
    Gf, If = np.fft.rfft(gt), np.fft.rfft(i_wave)
    return np.fft.irfft(np.conj(If) * Gf, gt.size) / gt.size   # Ω(θ) [rad/s]

i_sine = np.sqrt(2)*I_RMS*np.cos(X)                   # sine of the same I_rms
i_star = (I_RMS/gt_rms) * gt_p                        # [P3] Eq.(44), + sign
wl_sine = lock_characteristic(gt_p, i_sine).max()     # upper lock edge [rad/s]
wl_star = lock_characteristic(gt_p, i_star).max()     # should touch I_rms·Γ̃_rms

Verified output numbers (PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_39_optimal_injection.py):

print(gain_asym)                      # -> 1.0863 cos+0.3 matched gain = analytic sqrt(1+2α²)=1.0863
print(edges_asym)                     # -> +0.7681/-0.5338 matched(+) upper/lower edges (units of I_rms/q_max; sine ±0.7071)
print(gamma_rms_ring)                 # -> 0.05634 = [P2] Eq.(55) closed form 0.05634 (construction sanity check)
print(fL_sine_ring, fL_matched_ring)  # -> 0.1923 MHz, 0.3984 MHz N=17 ring toy, same I_rms=44.43 μA
print(gain_ring)                      # -> 2.0720 closed form sqrt(ηN/3)=2.0616 (0.5% difference = sinc² correction)
print(matched_over_bound)             # -> 1.0000 the matched injection exactly touches the Cauchy–Schwarz bound (all three cases)

How to read this figure: (a) the two waveforms have exactly the same rms (both 44.43 μA); the only difference is where the money goes — the matched injection (red) concentrates the current into narrow pulses shaped like the ISF, while the sine (blue dashed) spends most of its current in the dead zone where Γ~≈0\tilde\Gamma\approx0Γ~≈0; (b) the corresponding lock characteristics: the extrema are the lock edges, and the red curve exactly touches the dotted theoretical bound ±IrmsΓ~rms/2π=±398\pm I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}/2\pi=\pm398±Irms​Γ~rms​/2π=±398 kHz, while the sine only reaches 192 kHz — the same power, ×2.07 the lock range (and Part A's noise-suppression-bandwidth ceiling ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​ scales by ×2.07 along with it).

Conditions for validity and failure modes (this section)​

ConditionWhen it holdsWhat happens when it fails

V-H observation)
"Size" measured by IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ (Eq.(43))Optimum = Eq.(44), ceiling = Eq.(45)Change the constraint and the optimum changes: if the peak current is limited, ∣iinj∣≤Ipk\lvert i_{inj}\rvert\le I_{pk}∣iinj​∣≤Ipk​, the optimum becomes the square-like i=Ipk sign(Γ~)i=I_{pk}\,\mathrm{sign}(\tilde\Gamma)i=Ipk​sign(Γ~) with ceiling Ipk⟨∣Γ~∣⟩I_{pk}\langle\lvert\tilde\Gamma\rvert\rangleIpk​⟨∣Γ~∣⟩ (this site's extension, not in [P3])
The injector can generate the waveformFull GGG collectedNarrow pulses need bandwidth up to ∼N\sim N∼N harmonics: at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, a 17-stage pulse needs spectral content out to ~85 GHz — in practice the pulses are widened and GGG degrades smoothly along the ISF autocorrelation (no cliff)

The goal is the maximum lock rangeAll of this sectionSometimes you want to minimize it (multiple oscillators interfering, reducing coupling) — the same framework run in reverse ([P3] p.2120 closing explicitly flags this direction)

Three design sentences: (i) for LC (near-sine ISF), don't bother — a sinusoidal injection is already at the ceiling (exactly gain 1.0000 for a pure sine; the residual gain for near-sine ISFs is second-order small); (ii) ring/relaxation (pulse-type ISFs) benefit the most from waveform design, with gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​ growing as the square root of the stage count; (iii) this gain simultaneously scales Part A's ωc\omega_cωc​ — at the same power the noise-suppression-bandwidth ceiling also gains ×G, which is the number SerDes ILO deskew actually cares about.

Design knobs (rolling both parts into an actionable checklist)​

  1. Push Δω\Delta\omegaΔω to the center of the lock range: the noise-suppression bandwidth ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​ is only maximal at Δω=0\Delta\omega=0Δω=0. The goal of a calibration/tuning loop is not just "get locked," it's "get locked in the middle."
  2. Two ways to increase ωL\omega_LωL​ ([P3] Eq.(35): ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣): raise the injection current (at the cost of power and spurs), or use waveform design to align injection harmonics with ISF harmonics ([P3] Sec. VI's injection waveform design — effectively a free boost to ωL\omega_LωL​ and ωc\omega_cωc​; for the quantitative ceiling and the optimal waveform see the "Injection waveform design" section above: ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​, with gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​ for ring-type ISFs). Ceiling to watch: Iinj≪Imax=ω0qmaxI_{inj}\ll I_{max}=\omega_0 q_{max}Iinj​≪Imax​=ω0​qmax​ ([P3] Eq.(36)–(37)).
  3. Leave edge margin: the plateau penalty is 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​. ∣Δω∣/ωL=0.5\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert/\omega_L=0.5∣Δω∣/ωL​=0.5 only costs +1.2+1.2+1.2 dB; 0.950.950.95 costs +10.1+10.1+10.1 dB. Budget for PVT drift should be counted against Δω/ωL\Delta\omega/\omega_LΔω/ωL​.
  4. Recognize the fingerprint of pulling: a comb next to the carrier that is one-sided, evenly spaced by ωb\omega_bωb​, with one edge pinned exactly at some fixed frequency → that fixed frequency is the aggressor's frequency. Countermeasures, in order: add isolation (layout, guard ring, supply/substrate filtering); move the frequency plan (pull Δω\Delta\omegaΔω larger, so the comb spacing ωb→Δω\omega_b\to\Delta\omegaωb​→Δω moves further out and the amplitude r→0r\to0r→0 shrinks); or, conversely, just lock onto it deliberately (make ωL\omega_LωL​ larger than ∣Δω∣\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert∣Δω∣, so the spur comb collapses into a clean locked carrier). The most dangerous case is neither near nor far: when Δω\Delta\omegaΔω is only slightly above ωL\omega_LωL​, ωb\omega_bωb​ is tiny, the spur sits right next to the carrier (in-band, can't be filtered out) and r→1r\to1r→1 (slow decay, a dense, tall comb).
  5. Connection to SerDes: injection-locked clock distribution (forwarded-clock / multi-lane ILO deskew) is using ωc\omega_cωc​ as the jitter tracking bandwidth — reference jitter below ωc\omega_cωc​ is copied through (a benefit for lanes with common jitter: shared source, correlated cancellation), while above ωc\omega_cωc​ cleanliness relies on the local oscillator itself (the same old homework of qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, design_tradeoffs). The trade-off structure is exactly isomorphic to a CDR: see serdes_clocking_connection, lab_13.

Key takeaways​

  • Injection locking = a first-order PLL: linearizing [P3]'s generalized Adler gives d(δθ)/dt=−ωcδθ+nd(\delta\theta)/dt=-\omega_c\delta\theta+nd(δθ)/dt=−ωc​δθ+n, loop bandwidth ωc=ωLcos⁡θss=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL​cosθss​=ωL2​−Δω2​ — exactly the pull-in frequency of [P3] Eq.(40) (general topology: ωc=−Ω′(θss)\omega_c=-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})ωc​=−Ω′(θss​)).
  • Self-noise is high-passed, reference noise is low-passed, sharing the corner ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​; under a white FM drive, Sθ=Sn/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta=S_n/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​=Sn​/(ωc2​+ω2), low-frequency plateau Sn/ωc2S_n/\omega_c^2Sn​/ωc2​, finite total variance Sn/(4ωc)S_n/(4\omega_c)Sn​/(4ωc​) (simulation: corner and plateau both match theory to within 0.96-1.00×).
  • Suppression vanishes at the lock edge: as Δω→ωL\Delta\omega\to\omega_LΔω→ωL​, cos⁡θss→0\cos\theta_{ss}\to0cosθss​→0, the plateau rises as 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​ (+10.1+10.1+10.1 dB at 0.95 ωL0.95\,\omega_L0.95ωL​) — locked doesn't mean clean; margin must be budgeted.
  • When it doesn't lock: θ\thetaθ slides in a sawtooth (dwell + slip), beat frequency ωb=Δω2−ωL2\omega_b=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}ωb​=Δω2−ωL2​​ (derived step by step; [P4] Eq.(34)); the spectrum is a one-sided comb: lines at ωinj+kωb\omega_{inj}+k\omega_bωinj​+kωb​, one edge exactly at the injection frequency ([P4] Sec. V-B), amplitude decaying geometrically as r=ωL/(Δω+ωb)r=\omega_L/(\Delta\omega+\omega_b)r=ωL​/(Δω+ωb​) (external, Armand 1969; simulation matches −9.54-9.54−9.54 dB/line to the digit).
  • Two faces of the same square root: inside lock, ωL2−Δω2\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωL2​−Δω2​ = the noise-suppression corner; outside lock, Δω2−ωL2\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}Δω2−ωL2​​ = the spur comb spacing. In design, you want one of them large (wide suppression) and the other either large or zero (spur far away, or locked out entirely).
  • The ceiling of waveform design: at fixed IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ (= the proxy for injection power, [P3] Eq.(43)), the Cauchy–Schwarz ceiling of the lock range is ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​ ([P3] Eq.(45)), with equality ⟺ iinj∝Γ~i_{inj}\propto\tilde\Gammaiinj​∝Γ~ (Eq.(44), the ±\pm± selecting the upper/lower edge). Pure-sine ISF: a sine is already optimal (gain = 1.0000); ring-type pulse ISF: G≈ηN/3G\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}G≈ηN/3​, ×2.07 at N=17N=17N=17 — the same order as [P3] Fig. 19's "almost doubled."

External literature (not among the five downloaded source PDFs)​

  • [E-Adler] R. Adler, "A Study of Locking Phenomena in Oscillators," Proc. IRE, vol. 34, no. 6, pp. 351–357, Jun. 1946. (The original paper on the classical Adler equation and the beat phenomenon.)
  • [E-Kurokawa] K. Kurokawa, "Injection Locking of Microwave Solid-State Oscillators," Proc. IEEE, vol. 61, no. 10, pp. 1386–1410, Oct. 1973. (Noise shaping of injection-locked oscillators — the classic source for this page's Part A high-pass/low-pass result.)
  • [E-Armand] M. Armand, "On the Output Spectrum of Unlocked Driven Oscillators," Proc. IEEE, vol. 57, no. 5, pp. 798–799, May 1969. (Closed-form one-sided geometric comb spectrum of an unlocked driven oscillator — this page's Part B r=ωL/(Δω+ωb)r=\omega_L/(\Delta\omega+\omega_b)r=ωL​/(Δω+ωb​).)
  • [E-Razavi04] B. Razavi, "A Study of Injection Locking and Pulling in Oscillators," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 39, no. 9, pp. 1415–1424, Sep. 2004. (An accessible modern derivation and picture of the pulled spectrum; complements the ISF generalization of [P3]/[P4].)
  • Also: [P4] p.2130 points the noise analysis of locked/free-running oscillators to its own reference [29, Ch. 7] (B. Hong's PhD thesis).
